description: The question's literal reading is wrong. Its reading in the conversation is right. Earlier turns establish the setting, a web app where each request is a separate process. The last message says Python cannot pause at a line and resume there. Generators can pause and resume within a single process. In this setting they cannot, because a suspended generator does not survive a process boundary. A good answer affirms the user's claim within that setting.

history.content: I'm building an agent for the backend of the web app using the LangGraph framework, and I'm running into some issues with its human in the loop (HITL) implementation that I'd like to help with. To start, please do a little research on the langgraph framework to get familiar with it, and summarize your understanding for me in one to two paragraphs, so I can ensure that you understand it.

Here's my understanding of LangGraph, focused on the parts that matter for HITL. The framework. LangGraph models an agent as a state machine rather than a chain. You define a StateGraph over a typed state object (a TypedDict/Pydantic model), where each field can carry a reducer that says how updates merge — the common one being 'append to the message list' rather than 'overwrite.' Nodes are plain functions that take the  current state and return a partial update; edges connect them, and conditional edges route based on the returned state. A node can also return a Command to update state and  pick the next node in one step, and Send lets you fan out to many parallel copies of a node. Compiling the graph with a checkpointer makes execution durable: after every super-step the state is written to storage under a thread_id, so a conversation is just a thread you can re-invoke, inspect, fork, or rewind to an earlier checkpoint.

Human in the loop. HITL is built on that persistence. Inside a node you call interrupt(value), which raises a GraphInterrupt, saves state, and surfaces value to whoever invoked the graph — typically your HTTP handler, which returns it to the frontend as 'here's the tool call awaiting approval.' Later you re-invoke the same thread_id with Command(resume=answer), and answer becomes the return value of that interrupt() call. The gotcha that trips up most people: resuming re-runs the interrupted node from the  top, not from the interrupt line. Everything before the interrupt() executes a second time, so any DB write or API call there must be idempotent or must move after the interrupt. Related traps: interrupts in a node are matched to resume values by position, so the order and number of interrupt() calls must be stable across the re-run; wrapping interrupt() in a bare try/except swallows the control-flow exception; and the value passed must be JSON-serializable to survive the checkpointer. There's also an older static form — interrupt_before / interrupt_after on compile — which pauses at node boundaries and is meant for debugging, not for production approval flows.

input.task: Yes. My question is about the fact that resuming reruns the interrupted node from the top, not from the interrupt line. Why doesn't LangGraph run from the interrupt line? Is this a language level limitation? the human-in-the-loop feature cannot pause at a specific line, because Python doesn't have the ability to do that. Is that right?
